texts.0: SP, due to an attention bottleneck on the airspeed and AOA indications, stopped cross-checking the altimeter while establishing slow flight. SP did not trap the sink that developed when power was added late, and altitude departed more than 300 feet from the entry altitude. IP had to direct the recovery to regain the assigned altitude, and the margin above the minimum safe altitude required by the conditions was eroded.
texts.1: SP, due to a scan that dwelled on the airspeed indicator, checked the altimeter only at long intervals during slow flight. Altitude reached the 300 feet tolerance limit and SP began correcting only after verbal prompting from IP. The correction was then applied late and with a large pitch change instead of a small trimmed input.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed pitch and power cross-check at the entry, allowed altitude to drift about 200 feet from the entry altitude. SP detected the deviation without prompting and returned inside tolerance with a smooth trimmed correction, with no IP intervention required. The trend was nevertheless allowed to develop before it was recognized.
texts.3: SP maintained the entry altitude within 150 feet throughout slow flight. SP cross-checked the altimeter and VSI at short intervals and corrected the first trend with small pitch and power inputs. Altitude was held while airspeed and configuration were being managed.
texts.4: SP held the entry altitude with negligible excursion during the whole slow flight sequence. SP anticipated the pitch change required with each power and configuration change and trimmed the aircraft precisely. The altimeter remained essentially steady, including through the turns.
texts.marginal: SP maintained altitude inside standards, but the excursions repeatedly reached the upper half of the tolerance and were removed with one large input rather than several small ones. The trend is toward late detection of the sink whenever attention shifts to airspeed. SP is expected to shorten the altimeter cross-check interval and lead the required power change so that deviations are contained earlier.

texts.0: SP, due to imprecise power management at the target slow flight airspeed, did not stabilize the aircraft on the airspeed prescribed by the Techniques and Procedures Manual. Excursions exceeded the plus 15 and minus 5 knots tolerance, including a decay below the target that IP had to arrest with a power call and control input. SP did not re-establish a stabilized condition unaided.
texts.1: SP, due to coarse throttle inputs followed by over-correction, oscillated around the target airspeed. Excursions reached the plus 15 knots and minus 5 knots limits and SP reduced them only after IP verbally identified the trend. Recovery to the target airspeed was slow and the aircraft never settled for more than a few seconds.
texts.2: SP, due to a power setting selected without reference to the pitch attitude required, allowed airspeed to run about 10 knots fast and briefly 2 to 3 knots slow. SP recognized the deviation and re-established the target airspeed with a single corrected power adjustment, without IP intervention. Time spent outside the tighter tolerance was short.
texts.3: SP established and maintained the slow flight airspeed within plus 5 and minus 0 knots. Power was set positively to the value required and refined in small increments while pitch was held with trim. Airspeed remained stable through the heading changes.
texts.4: SP flew the slow flight airspeed with negligible variation from the target and never allowed it to decay below the prescribed value. Power and pitch were coordinated so that each change was anticipated rather than chased. The condition was stabilized within a few seconds of entry and held there.
texts.marginal: SP kept airspeed inside standards but consistently on the fast side, using excess speed as a margin instead of flying the prescribed value. The trend is toward correcting with throttle alone while the pitch attitude is left unchecked. SP is expected to set the required pitch attitude first and use small power adjustments so that the target airspeed is held precisely.

texts.0: SP, due to uncoordinated rudder use at high angle of attack and low airspeed, did not hold the reference heading during slow flight. Heading wandered beyond 10 degrees and continued to diverge while SP concentrated on airspeed. IP had to take corrective action to return the aircraft to the reference heading.
texts.1: SP, due to reliance on the attitude indicator without reference to the heading indication, allowed heading to reach the 10 degrees tolerance limit. SP started the correction only after IP prompted, and then used aileron without matching rudder, so the heading overshot on recapture.
texts.2: SP, due to residual yaw left uncorrected after each power change, drifted about 8 degrees from the reference heading. SP identified the drift on the next cross-check and returned to heading with coordinated aileron and rudder, without IP intervention. The correction was timely, but the yaw had been allowed to build first.
texts.3: SP maintained the reference heading within 5 degrees throughout slow flight. Rudder was applied with each power change to keep the ball centered and the heading steady. Corrections were small, coordinated and immediate.
texts.4: SP held the reference heading with negligible wander during slow flight and through the configuration changes. SP anticipated the yaw associated with each power change and applied rudder before the heading moved. Coordination remained precise at the low airspeed.
texts.marginal: SP held heading inside standards, but the aircraft was allowed to yaw before the rudder input was made and the ball was often off center. The trend is toward correcting heading with bank rather than with coordinated rudder. SP is expected to lead each power change with rudder so that heading is maintained without banking.

texts.0: SP, due to over-controlling in roll at the low airspeed, did not maintain the bank angle called for in the maneuver. Bank exceeded the 10 degrees tolerance and was allowed to increase while airspeed was decaying, which reduced the margin above the stall. IP intervened to level the wings and restore the flight condition.
texts.1: SP, due to large aileron inputs made without a fixed outside reference, allowed bank to reach the 10 degrees tolerance. SP stabilized the bank only after IP called the deviation, and the correction produced a roll oscillation before the wings settled.
texts.2: SP, due to a lag in checking roll once the turn was established, allowed bank to vary by about 8 degrees around the required angle. SP noticed the variation and stabilized the bank with a small aileron input, without IP intervention. The turns were completed inside the flight parameters.
texts.3: SP maintained bank within 5 degrees of the required angle during the slow flight turns. Roll inputs were small and the bank was checked against both the attitude indicator and the horizon. Turns were entered and stopped precisely.
texts.4: SP held bank with negligible variation and rolled into and out of each turn at a constant rate. The wings were stabilized immediately on the required angle without hunting. Bank was controlled with no associated loss of altitude or airspeed.
texts.marginal: SP kept bank inside standards but let it creep above the required angle in the turn before checking it. The trend is toward reactive rather than anticipatory roll control at low airspeed. SP is expected to stabilize the bank angle on entry to the turn and check it against a fixed reference so that it does not wander.

texts.0: SP, due to inadequate workload management during the entry, did not execute slow flight as described in the Techniques and Procedures Manual. SP made configuration and power changes out of order and omitted required checks, so the aircraft was never stabilized in the prescribed condition and parameters went beyond tolerance in more than one axis. IP had to direct the sequence and take the controls to re-establish the entry.
texts.1: SP, due to task saturation once power was reduced, executed the entry steps late and out of the briefed order. SP completed the sequence only after IP prompted each remaining item, and the aircraft reached the slow flight condition well after the point required. Parameters had to be recovered from the tolerance limit.
texts.2: SP, due to attention divided between configuring the aircraft and holding the parameters, reversed two steps of the entry sequence. SP recognized the omission, completed the missing item and stabilized the aircraft inside the flight parameters without IP intervention. Entry took longer than required, but the maneuver was flown as described in the manual.
texts.3: SP executed slow flight in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual. Configuration, power and trim changes were made in the correct order and at the correct points, and the required checks were completed. The aircraft was stabilized in the prescribed condition promptly.
texts.4: SP executed the slow flight sequence exactly as described in the manual, with each configuration and power change anticipated and trimmed before the next step was taken. Checks were completed without interrupting the flight parameters. The aircraft was stabilized in the prescribed condition immediately on entry.
texts.marginal: SP followed the prescribed sequence but needed most of the available attention to do so, and the parameters loosened at each configuration change. The trend is toward handling flying and configuring one after the other rather than together. SP is expected to consolidate the sequence to the point where the aircraft can be configured while the parameters are held unchanged.

texts.0: SP, due to flying the maneuver untrimmed, did not apply the pitch and power technique described in the Techniques and Procedures Manual. SP held large control forces, which produced coupled altitude and airspeed excursions outside tolerance in both axes. IP had to take the controls to re-trim the aircraft and re-establish the condition.
texts.1: SP, due to trimming only after each deviation had developed, held the aircraft in slow flight with continuous control pressure. Parameters reached their tolerance limits and were corrected only after IP verbally prompted a trim change. Control inputs remained coarse for the remainder of the maneuver.
texts.2: SP, due to trim applied in one large step rather than progressively, allowed pitch to wander after the power change. SP recognized the residual control force, retrimmed and stabilized the aircraft inside the flight parameters without IP intervention. The technique was correct but applied late.
texts.3: SP flew slow flight with the aircraft trimmed for the condition, using pitch for flight path and power for airspeed as described in the manual. Control inputs were small and smooth at the low airspeed. The aircraft remained stabilized with minimal control pressure.
texts.4: SP trimmed the aircraft precisely for the slow flight condition and kept it trimmed through every power and configuration change. Inputs were anticipatory, small and smooth, and no control force was carried. The aircraft remained stabilized throughout with no parameter chasing.
texts.marginal: SP used the correct technique but carried a light out-of-trim force for much of the maneuver, which showed as slow pitch wander. The trend is toward substituting elevator pressure for trim at low airspeed. SP is expected to trim immediately after each power change so that the aircraft holds the condition without sustained control pressure.

error_modes.label: STALL MARGIN AND AVOIDANCE OF STALL CHARACTERISTICS

texts.0: SP, due to inadequate monitoring and cross-check of airspeed and AOA, allowed the inadvertent appearance of stall characteristics during slow flight. SP did not respond to the stall warning and buffet, airspeed fell below the minus 5 knots tolerance and the aircraft was allowed to approach a departure from the prescribed condition. IP took the controls to recover and the maneuver was terminated.
texts.1: SP, due to a cross-check that did not include the AOA indication, let airspeed decay to the minus 5 knots limit until the stall warning activated. SP relieved the condition only after IP called it, and the recovery was made with a large pitch reduction that cost altitude out to the tolerance limit.
texts.2: SP, due to a slow response to the first buffet cue, allowed the angle of attack to increase toward the low end of the airspeed tolerance. SP recognized the cue without prompting, added power and reduced angle of attack before any further stall characteristic developed, keeping the aircraft inside the flight parameters. No IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP flew slow flight without allowing the inadvertent appearance of stall characteristics. SP monitored airspeed and AOA continuously and used power to keep a positive margin above the stall. The aircraft was kept clear of buffet throughout the maneuver.
texts.4: SP maintained a deliberate and consistent margin above the stall throughout slow flight, with no buffet or warning at any point. SP cross-checked AOA together with airspeed continuously and adjusted power before the margin could erode, including in the turns. Awareness of the stall margin was evident in every control input.
texts.marginal: SP avoided stall characteristics, but the margin above the stall stayed thin, particularly in the turns where the angle of attack was allowed to increase. The trend is toward monitoring airspeed alone instead of airspeed together with AOA. SP is expected to include the AOA indication in every cross-check and to use power earlier to protect the margin.

error_modes.label: CLEARING, ALTITUDE BLOCK AND OUTSIDE AWARENESS

texts.0: SP, due to attention held inside the cockpit, did not clear the area or confirm the minimum safe altitude before entering slow flight. SP entered below the minimum safe altitude determined in the Techniques and Procedures Manual and did not monitor the aircraft position relative to the area boundaries. IP had to direct a repositioning before the maneuver could be flown.
texts.1: SP, due to an abbreviated clearing turn and a single check of the altitude, entered slow flight at the lower limit of the altitude required. SP corrected the entry altitude and resumed lookout only after IP prompted, and awareness of the area boundary remained weak for the rest of the maneuver.
texts.2: SP, due to a clearing scan that covered the turn direction but not the whole area, began the entry with an incomplete lookout. SP recognized the omission, completed the clearing and confirmed the altitude before establishing slow flight, without IP intervention. The maneuver was then flown inside the flight parameters.
texts.3: SP cleared the area, confirmed the minimum safe altitude and set the entry altitude before establishing slow flight. SP maintained lookout and awareness of the area boundaries and of the aircraft position throughout the maneuver, in the day VMC conditions required.
texts.4: SP cleared the area thoroughly, confirmed the altitude available and briefed the entry before establishing slow flight. SP maintained an unbroken lookout and continuous awareness of position, altitude margin and traffic while flying precise parameters. Attention was divided between the maneuver and the environment with neither degraded.
texts.marginal: SP cleared the area and respected the altitude limits, but the lookout narrowed once the maneuver was established and most of the scan stayed inside the cockpit. The trend is toward trading outside awareness for parameter precision. SP is expected to keep a deliberate external scan through the whole maneuver, including during the turns.

error_modes.label: ADVERSE YAW AND COORDINATED RUDDER IN THE TURNS

texts.0: SP, due to rolling into and out of the turns without coordinated rudder, did not track the nose onto the selected reference point during the adverse yaw demonstration. The nose continued well past the rollout point and the resulting weaving, the S-ing described in the manual, drove heading and bank beyond the 10 degree tolerance while the yaw was left uncorrected. IP had to take the controls to centre the ball and re-establish coordinated slow flight.
texts.1: SP, due to using aileron alone to roll into the 20 degree bank turns, allowed the initial adverse yaw to swing the nose away from the direction of turn. Heading and bank reached the 10 degree tolerance limit and the ball was recentred only after IP verbally called for rudder. The nose still overshot the selected rollout point on the following turn.
texts.2: SP, due to rudder applied after the aileron rather than with it, allowed the nose to yaw off the reference point on the first roll-in. Deviation reached about 7 degrees in heading and bank before SP recognised the uncoordinated condition, added rudder and stopped the nose on the rollout point without IP intervention. Coordination was correct for the remaining turns.
texts.3: SP rolled into and out of the turns with rudder coordinated with aileron, so the nose tracked immediately and stopped on the selected rollout point. Heading and bank stayed within 5 degrees of the intended values and the ball remained centred. The difference between the uncoordinated and coordinated rolls was demonstrated as described in the manual.
texts.4: SP led every roll with coordinated rudder, so no adverse yaw was allowed to develop at any point of the demonstration. The nose tracked the reference points precisely, heading and bank showed negligible deviation and the ball did not move off centre. SP also applied the greater rudder deflection required for the right turns without prompting.
texts.marginal: SP kept heading and bank inside standards, but the rudder consistently trailed the aileron and small yaw excursions appeared on each roll-in. The trend is toward flying the turns with aileron first and correcting the yaw afterwards, which is the mechanism that produces weaving on final. SP is expected to apply rudder together with aileron so that the nose tracks onto the rollout point without a correction.

error_modes.label: TORQUE EFFECTS AND NOSE TRACK ON POWER APPLICATION

texts.0: SP, due to not maintaining positive control when power was advanced to MAX from slow flight, allowed the aircraft to pitch up, yaw and roll left as described for the torque demonstration. SP did not hold the takeoff pitch attitude or apply the right rudder required, so bank and heading departed beyond 10 degrees and the aircraft approached the stall with the stick shaker active. IP took the controls to arrest the left roll and recover.
texts.1: SP, due to applying MAX power without leading it with right rudder, let the nose track up and left on the power application. Bank and heading reached the 10 degree tolerance limit and the nose was brought back only after IP called for rudder and pitch. The same tendency reappeared when power was reduced and the nose dropped and yawed right.
texts.2: SP, due to rudder applied only after the yaw was seen rather than with the power, allowed the nose to track left of the intended point. The deviation reached about 7 degrees in heading and bank before SP added right rudder, held the takeoff pitch attitude and returned the nose track to the reference without IP intervention. Control was regained promptly but the input was reactive.
texts.3: SP held the proper takeoff pitch attitude and applied coordinated right rudder as power was advanced, keeping the nose tracking straight. Heading and bank stayed within 5 degrees throughout the power application and the subsequent reduction to idle. Positive control of the aircraft was maintained in both directions of power change.
texts.4: SP anticipated the pitch up, yaw and left roll tendency and countered it with rudder and pitch as the power was moved, so the nose track never deviated. Heading and bank showed negligible change through the full power application and reduction. SP also verbalised the torque effect being demonstrated while flying it precisely.
texts.marginal: SP kept the nose track inside standards, but each power change produced a visible left yaw that was removed after the fact rather than prevented. The trend is toward treating the rudder as a correction instead of leading the power with it. SP is expected to apply right rudder as the power moves so that the nose track stays constant, as required for takeoffs and touch-and-go landings.

error_modes.label: STEEP TURN AT SLOW AIRSPEED AND AOA CONTROL

texts.0: SP, due to increasing bank towards 60 degrees without adding the power and back pressure required to maintain level flight, allowed the angle of attack to rise into a stall during the steep turn demonstration. SP did not roll out of the bank to recover from the impending stall, so altitude departed more than 300 feet and airspeed decayed more than 5 knots below the target. IP took the controls to reduce bank and recover the aircraft.
texts.1: SP, due to increasing bank faster than power and back pressure were added, let the nose fall and the angle of attack build in the steep turn. Altitude reached the 300 feet tolerance limit and airspeed the 5 knots low limit, and the bank was reduced only after IP called the impending stall. The recovery was made with a large control input rather than a controlled rollout.
texts.2: SP, due to back pressure applied ahead of the power increase while rolling towards 60 degrees of bank, allowed the angle of attack to increase and altitude to drop about 200 feet. SP recognised the buffet, rolled out of the bank to relieve the condition and re-established level slow flight without IP intervention. The entry into the steep turn remained the source of the deviation.
texts.3: SP increased bank towards 60 degrees slowly while adding power and back pressure together, holding altitude within 150 feet and airspeed within the plus 5 and minus 0 knots tolerance. SP monitored the angle of attack as it increased and rolled out of the bank at the impending stall as described in the manual. The wingtip pivot around the ground reference was observed as intended.
texts.4: SP flew the steep turn with bank, power and back pressure increased together, so altitude and airspeed showed negligible deviation throughout. SP tracked the angle of attack build precisely and initiated the rollout at the impending stall without any excursion or abrupt input. The demonstration of reduced turning radius against increased turn rate was flown exactly as briefed.
texts.marginal: SP stayed inside standards, but the power and back pressure were added late relative to the bank, so the aircraft sank and the angle of attack rose more than necessary before the correction. The trend is toward leading with bank at an airspeed where the angle of attack increases quickly. SP is expected to increase power and back pressure with the bank so that level flight is preserved throughout the turn.

error_modes.label: ABRUPT CONTROL MOVEMENT AND SIMULATED FLARE SNATCH

texts.0: SP, due to holding the abrupt back stick pressure after reaching 20 degrees nose-high in the simulated flare snatch, allowed the angle of attack to increase into a full stall. SP did not release the backpressure to recover, and the resulting pitch excursion and sink cost more than 300 feet with airspeed well below the low tolerance. IP took the controls to unload the aircraft and recover.
texts.1: SP, due to a delayed release of backpressure after the abrupt nose-high input, let the aircraft progress towards a full stall with the stick shaker active. Altitude reached the 300 feet tolerance limit and airspeed the 5 knots low limit, and the control was unloaded only after IP called for it. The recovery input was then as abrupt as the entry.
texts.2: SP, due to recognising the rapid angle of attack build a moment late, allowed the pitch excursion to develop before releasing backpressure. Altitude deviated about 200 feet and airspeed briefly ran low before SP recovered the condition without IP intervention. The lesson of snatching the control stick in the flare was demonstrated but the recovery was reactive.
texts.3: SP applied the abrupt back stick pressure to 20 degrees nose-high as briefed and released it at the first indication of the rapid angle of attack increase. Altitude was contained within 150 feet and airspeed remained inside the plus 5 and minus 0 knots tolerance. SP identified the effect of an abrupt flare on the sink rate.
texts.4: SP flew the abrupt control movement demonstration deliberately and recovered by releasing backpressure the instant the angle of attack began to rise, with negligible altitude and airspeed excursion. SP related the demonstration to fixation on the aim point during landing and to viewing the total landing environment. Control was smooth and positive throughout the recovery.
texts.marginal: SP contained the excursion inside standards, but the backpressure was released late and the recovery itself was made with a sharp forward input. The trend is toward matching one abrupt input with another instead of applying controls in a smooth, positive manner. SP is expected to unload the aircraft at the first angle of attack cue and to fly the recovery smoothly.

texts.0: SP, due to raising the flaps from LDG to UP without increasing pitch attitude to maintain altitude, allowed the loss of lift and sink rate that the manual associates with flap retraction below the recommended airspeed. SP did not reselect LDG flaps to recover when the angle of attack increased and the aircraft stalled, and altitude departed more than 300 feet. IP took the controls to recover the aircraft and re-establish the block.
texts.1: SP, due to retracting the flaps before setting the pitch attitude required, let the sink rate develop and the angle of attack increase towards the stall. Altitude reached the 300 feet tolerance limit and LDG flaps were reselected only after IP directed the recovery. The initial airspeed increase was not used to lead the pitch change.
texts.2: SP, due to increasing pitch attitude only after the sink had started during the flap retraction, allowed altitude to drop about 200 feet. SP recognised the angle of attack increase, selected LDG flaps to alleviate the condition and re-established slow flight without IP intervention. The demonstration was completed but the pitch change lagged the configuration change.
texts.3: SP raised the flaps from LDG to UP without pausing at TO and increased pitch attitude as they retracted, holding altitude within 150 feet. SP recognised the angle of attack increase as the flaps reached UP and recovered by selecting LDG flaps as described in the manual. Airspeed stayed inside the plus 5 and minus 0 knots tolerance.
texts.4: SP led the flap retraction with the pitch attitude required, so altitude showed negligible change while the flaps travelled and the initial airspeed increase was absorbed. SP identified the stall onset immediately and alleviated it by reselecting LDG flaps with no secondary excursion. The relationship between configuration, lift and angle of attack was demonstrated precisely.
texts.marginal: SP held the parameters inside standards, but the pitch input trailed the flap travel and a sink rate was allowed to appear before it was trapped. The trend is toward reacting to the configuration change rather than anticipating the lift loss. SP is expected to set the pitch attitude as the flaps start to move so that no sink rate develops.

error_modes.label: CONTROL EFFECTIVENESS AND SMOOTHNESS OF INPUTS

texts.0: SP, due to flying slow flight with rapid, snatched control inputs, did not allow the aircraft time to respond at an airspeed where there is little airflow over the control surfaces. SP chased each indication with a larger input than the last, so altitude and bank oscillated beyond the 300 feet and 10 degree tolerances without settling. IP had to take the controls to damp the oscillation and re-establish a stabilised condition.
texts.1: SP, due to small rapid stick movements instead of smooth, positive inputs, produced a continuous pitch and roll oscillation in slow flight. Altitude and bank reached their tolerance limits and the inputs were softened only after IP verbally identified the over-control. The aircraft was never allowed to settle between corrections.
texts.2: SP, due to inputs made faster than the reduced control effectiveness allowed, over-controlled the first two corrections in slow flight. Bank varied about 7 degrees and altitude about 200 feet before SP slowed the inputs, let the aircraft respond and stabilised the condition without IP intervention. The over-control was recognised and removed by SP.
texts.3: SP flew slow flight with smooth, positive control inputs and waited for the aircraft to respond before adding more. Bank stayed within 5 degrees and altitude within 150 feet with no oscillation. SP noted the reduced control effectiveness demonstrated by the rapid aileron movements.
texts.4: SP applied every input smoothly and positively and sized it correctly for the reduced control effectiveness, so no over-control appeared at any stage. Bank and altitude showed negligible variation and the aircraft remained stabilised between the demonstrations. SP was able to describe the reduced authority while continuing to fly it accurately.
texts.marginal: SP kept the parameters inside standards, but the inputs remained quick and were followed by an immediate opposite correction. The trend is toward over-controlling at an airspeed where the aircraft needs time to respond. SP is expected to make one smooth, positive input, allow the aircraft to answer it, and only then refine the correction.

error_modes.label: SLOW-FLIGHT STALL RECOVERY BY ALLEVIATING THE CAUSING CONDITION

texts.0: SP, due to not identifying which condition had produced the stall, did not alleviate it by decreasing angle of attack, lowering the flaps or decreasing bank as the manual requires during slow flight. SP also did not initiate traffic pattern stall recovery procedures when the stall condition was not immediately corrected, and altitude departed more than 300 feet with airspeed below the low tolerance. IP took the controls and recovered the aircraft.
texts.1: SP, due to applying a generic pitch and power response instead of removing the specific cause, left the stalled condition in place through the first attempt. The recovery was completed only after IP named the condition to be alleviated, and altitude reached the 300 feet tolerance limit. SP did not recognise the point at which traffic pattern stall recovery procedures were required.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed diagnosis of the causing condition, alleviated the stall about two seconds after the indication appeared. SP decreased the angle of attack and reduced bank without IP intervention and altitude deviated about 200 feet before the aircraft was re-established in slow flight. The correct method was used but the recognition lagged.
texts.3: SP recovered each induced stall by alleviating the condition that caused it, decreasing angle of attack, lowering flaps or decreasing bank as appropriate. Altitude was held within 150 feet and airspeed within the plus 5 and minus 0 knots tolerance during the recoveries. SP applied this method only within slow flight, as the manual specifies.
texts.4: SP identified the causing condition immediately at every stall indication and removed it with a single accurate action, with negligible altitude and airspeed excursion. SP stated that this method applies only during slow flight and that a stall condition not immediately corrected requires traffic pattern stall recovery procedures. Each recovery was flown smoothly and without secondary deviation.
texts.marginal: SP recovered inside standards, but tended to add power first and only then remove the condition that had caused the stall. The trend is toward a habitual response rather than a diagnosis of the specific cause. SP is expected to identify and alleviate the causing condition first, and to move to traffic pattern stall recovery procedures if the condition is not immediately corrected.
